% ------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{What the case study can and cannot show}
% ------------------------------------------------------------

The carbon-capture slice is small wherever it is tightly defined. Only
\statCcAlignNCities{} cities carry enough carbon-capture papers and projects to run
the alignment test, too few to support a statistical argument on their own. The
broader tagging reaches further, across \statCcPartsNCities{} cities for the
part-type comparison, but that comparison returns a null. The slice trades power for
legibility. It lets us name the enzymes, follow one project's parts into the
literature, and watch the alignment result reappear in a corner small enough to
inspect by hand.

Read that way, the case study earns its place. It cannot prove that carbon-capture
innovation follows a local path. It can show what such a path looks like where it
exists, in a theme concrete enough that a reader can check the pieces against the
biology they already know.

% ============================================================
\section{Reproducibility and deliverables}
% ============================================================

A result is only as trustworthy as the path to it, so the whole analysis is built
to be re-run. The pipeline is a single notebook, one cell per step: ingest the
papers, projects, and parts; embed them; reduce and cluster the space; label the
clusters; and export the tables and figures this manuscript reads. Each step caches
its output, so a run that stops halfway resumes where it left off, and an expensive
stage never repeats without reason. Anyone with the repository and an API key can
rebuild every number in this draft from the raw sources.

The reusable logic lives in a small set of Python modules, one for each job:
ingesting each source, embedding, clustering, geocoding, and enforcing the shared
schema. The notebooks call these modules and hide no logic of their own. Keeping
the machinery in modules and the narrative in notebooks lets a reader follow the
story in one place and audit the implementation in another.

Configuration is explicit, and secrets stay out of the repository. The parameters
that shape the analysis, the embedding model, the clustering thresholds, the
retrieval terms, sit in a single settings file, so changing the study never means
hunting through code. API keys live in a local environment file that is never
committed, with an example file showing what a collaborator needs to supply.

The public-facing home for all of this is a documentation website, built with
Quarto and hosted on GitHub Pages. It gathers the background, the methods, the
results, the case study, and the reproducibility materials into one navigable
place, and offers the manuscript and slides for download. The site is the top-level
product; this manuscript is one of the things it points to.

Two interactive views do what a static page cannot. A semantic-space explorer plots
every artifact in the shared embedding, coloured by type and filterable down to the
carbon-capture subset, so a reader can pan through the field and see where projects,
papers, and parts fall. A geographic view puts the same data on a map, letting a
reader pick a city and read off its topical mix. Because GitHub Pages serves static
files, both are precomputed into small JSON exports and drawn in the browser, with
no server behind them.

Everything is public. The code, the notebooks, the manuscript source, and the
export scripts live in one repository at
\url{https://github.com/Zer0Juice/synbiomap}, and the rendered site sits at
\url{https://zer0juice.github.io/synbiomap}. The visualisation step writes the small
JSON files the site reads, the same files that back the two interactive views, so
the website and this manuscript draw from one set of exported artifacts, not two
diverging copies.

% ============================================================
\section{Discussion}
% ============================================================

It is worth being precise about what these measures see. Cosine similarity between
two city centroids is mostly a measure of field membership. Because every document
is synthetic biology, two cities look alike first because they share a field, and
only second because they share a local niche. That is why the raw overlap sits so
high, near \statOverlapMean{} for most cities, and why on its own it says little: a
number that starts near its ceiling for everyone cannot carry much about any one
place.

The permutation tests are what separate the two. When we shuffle which city's
projects face which city's papers within a country and the centroid overlap barely
moves, the high baseline shows itself to be a property of the field, not of local
alignment. The same shuffle applied to cluster co-membership tells the opposite
story: the observed value sits far out in the tail of the null. One measure fails
the test and one passes, and that difference is the whole argument. Field-level
similarity is real but uninformative; niche-level co-membership is what carries the
local signal.

The signal is not symmetric, and the asymmetry is a clue. A city's local alignment
tracks its volume of papers more than its volume of projects, and the
difference-in-differences leaves the papers looking like the fixed backdrop that
projects move against. The natural reading is directional: the academic literature
sets a city's niche, and the student projects settle into it, not the other way
around.

A simple mechanism would produce exactly this. iGEM teams are mentored by local
faculty, and those same faculty publish the city's papers. A professor working on
carbon fixation seeds a team with a carbon-fixation project and, in the same years,
publishes carbon-fixation papers. No idea has to flow from student to scholar for
the two to line up; a shared mentor puts them in the same niche from the start.
This is why we read co-membership as relatedness, not as a pipeline, and why the
mentor--student link is the first thing a follow-up study should measure.

This places the work beside the relatedness literature it borrows from.
\citet{boschmaScientificKnowledgeDynamics2014} found that biotech cities grow into
scientifically related areas over time; we find the same relatedness holding across
a boundary that literature has not crossed, between student projects and
professional research in one field. The contribution is less a new principle than a
new place to see the old one: relatedness measured from the text of what people
write, between artifacts that do not trade, cite, or hire across the gap we measure.

The methodological lesson generalises past this dataset. When a corpus is confined
to one field, cosine similarity between aggregates is dominated by the field, and a
naive regression on those similarities will light up with significance that means
nothing. A conventional reading of the stars would have reported a strong result.
Only the permutation test, which rebuilds the null from the data's own structure,
catches that the result is a baseline in disguise. Anyone measuring relatedness
inside a narrow domain should assume the baseline is there until a shuffle proves
otherwise.

% ============================================================
\section{Limitations}
% ============================================================

Several limits bound what this draft can claim, and most trace to one root: the
corpus is a single field. That is what pins the centroid overlap near its ceiling,
what forces us onto the sharper within-city measures, and what leaves even the
strongest result speaking to relatedness inside synthetic biology, not to synthetic
biology's place among other fields. A study spanning several fields would escape
this baseline, though it would answer a different question.

Two data limits compound it. Time resolution is coarse: a city-year centroid is
often built from a single document, too thin to carry the lead--lag signal the
temporal test went looking for. And place is flattened: each artifact is geocoded
to one affiliation, so a team split across two universities in two cities, or a
paper with authors in three, collapses to a single dot. Both blur exactly the fine
structure a stronger version of this study would resolve.

The associations we report are open to confounders we do not control. A city's
research base, the prestige of its universities, the presence of an established
biotech cluster, local funding and policy, all could raise both its student and its
academic output together without either touching the other. We measure that they
move together. We do not measure why, and the mentor-coupling story of the
Discussion is a hypothesis, not a result.

Finally, two tools are used past their design. SPECTER2 was trained on paper
abstracts and their citations, not on student wikis or patents, so applying it to
those artifacts assumes a transfer we cannot fully verify. And the cross-modal
counts undercount: a full-text search for BioBrick identifiers finds only
open-access, indexed papers, and the identifiers contain underscores that many
search systems mishandle, so the true number of parts-citing papers is larger than
the one we can see.

% ============================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% ============================================================

The question this draft set out to answer was whether cities that host student
synthetic biology projects also produce academic papers in related areas. The
answer is a qualified yes. Its strongest form is topical: in cities active enough to
measure it, a city's projects and papers fall in the \textit{same specific}
sub-fields far more than a same-country neighbour's would (cluster co-membership,
permutation $p = \statClusterPermP{}$), and that relatedness holds up after
stripping out both the field-level baseline and city size. The centroid-based tests
tell the same story from a second angle. A city's iGEM projects sit measurably
nearer its own papers than other cities' papers. The pattern holds across roughly
nine in ten projects and, more tellingly, across four in five \textit{cities} once
the inference is clustered where it belongs. It is strongest in large, mature hubs
but stays positive in the long tail, it reappears essentially unchanged in the
carbon-capture case, and it is echoed by a parts-based fingerprint that never
touches the embedding model. Cities do appear to specialise, and their student and
academic work specialises together.

Two qualifications, developed in the Discussion and Limitations, keep that finding
honest. The alignment is mostly a city's standing identity, not a year-by-year
coupling, so we call the local innovation trajectory shared specialisation, not a
demonstrated flow of ideas from students to scholars. And the strongest temporal
claim, that projects run ahead of papers, stays unresolved: the city-year centroids
are too thin to settle it, and settling it will take the finer instrument we turn
to now.

These limits also point the way forward, and mark where the project's remaining
reach comes in: patents, and the planet-scale application that motivates the whole
effort. The clearest gains would come from finer links than centroids can provide.
We could scrape the DOIs that iGEM teams cite on their wikis, building a direct
citation network between projects and the local literature. We could match paper,
patent, and team authors, and ask whether researchers stay in the orbit of their
old iGEM collaborators. We could match BioBrick sequences to patent filings through
sequence databases, tracing individual pieces of genetic code from an open registry
into commercial use. Each would replace a coarse, centroid-level association with a
concrete, traceable link, and let a future study move past whether a city's projects
and papers are related to whether one actually grew out of the other.
